analysis.title: Cross-Asset Weekly: Mind the gap
key_insights: Since 2007 the US economy has grown 49% versus 22% for the euro area, 43% for Switzerland and 30% for the UK. Demographics and immigration explain part of it, but US labour productivity (GDP per hour worked) has also grown much faster, especially since the pandemic.

Pandemic policy differed. The US raised unemployment benefits by USD 600 a week and sent stimulus checks but did little to protect jobs, so unemployment rose from 3.5% to 14.8%. Europe used short-time work schemes. The bank argues the US reshuffling moved workers into more productive sectors, while European schemes preserved existing structures and slowed hiring in growing sectors.

Gross fixed capital formation has grown far less in the euro area, where strict dismissal rules protect employees, than in the US, UK and Switzerland. The bank says energy is also a factor: Europe imports energy while the US has been a net energy exporter since 2019. Germany's terms of trade fell 1% between January 2020 and July 2026, while the US's rose 10%.

The bank expects the productivity gap to widen rather than close. Draghi report reforms need coordination among like-minded policymakers, and fragmented parliaments and populist leaders make that harder.

China's economy is K-shaped: October industrial production slowed to 4.8% from 5.5% in September, while hi-tech manufacturing accelerated to 17.6% y/y on the AI-driven export boom. Fixed asset investment is falling and retail sales are barely growing, with auto sales a large part of the weakness. Service production grew 4.6%.

China should meet its 4.5% 2026 growth target without new stimulus. Government bond issuance is backloaded and the September lending instrument is unused, leaving room to raise investment in 2027. Officials remain cautious ahead of the Party Congress in late 2027.

The bank is neutral on Chinese equities at index level and would turn more positive only with decisive stimulus for consumption or the housing market. MSCI China is down 20.7% in 2026 (as of 18 Nov), the worst major index, and has lagged Asia Pacific by 25.4 points. Forward P/E is 9.4x against a historical average of about 11x and extremes of 8x or below.
Tighter US export controls on advanced AI chips will likely weigh on Chinese AI labs in the near term but may help selected domestic Chinese semiconductor firms.

Cyclicals (industrials, materials, consumer discretionary) have underperformed defensives (utilities, staples, health care) by over 12% in three months. That has happened only twice in ten years, March 2020 and July 2022, both market troughs, yet the S&P 500 is only about 6% below its peak and 4% below pre-election levels. This time defensives rose rather than cyclicals falling.

Defensives trade at 19x 12-month forward EPS, the top of their historical range. The bank advises reducing defensive exposure, specifically consumer staples, utilities and Swiss equities, which it rates 'most preferred'. It prefers quality in a relative allocation and warns against buying the dip too early.

Tech and its sub-sectors rank better on EPS revisions and valuation, but the bank would add only on a relative basis and in the highest-quality names. It likes communication services (Meta, Google, telecoms). It stays cautious on banks because of valuations, a slowing cycle and offloading of data centre risk.

Credit spreads have widened in CCC and now in broader high yield. The bank says this is less likely to reverse quickly than in April 2025 because it comes with weaker fundamentals and monetary tightening. The equity risk premium over Treasuries has risen from zero to 50bps but is still historically depressed.
The Fed's senior loan officer survey shows US banks tightened business lending conditions in Q3 for the first time since 2024.

The Fed started raising rates again in September and will likely continue. October CPI showed inflation pressures rising and broadening. Because core CPI lags the cycle by about 10 months, the bank expects no easing before the end of Q1 2027.
The bank expects the cycle to slow significantly over coming quarters. Cyclicals may offer tactical opportunities but are unlikely to deliver sustained performance until the cycle bottoms.

The bank is cautious. Valuations are not compelling, lending conditions are tightening and it sees the best of the cycle behind banks.
Valuations are more attractive relative to defensives but not priced for a slowdown. Tactical opportunities only, with no sustained performance until the cycle bottoms.

earnings_insights: China's earnings outlook is the weakest in Asia Pacific. Industrial profits are strong in electronics, chemicals and mining and weak in domestically oriented sectors.
Defensives trade at 19x 12-month forward EPS, the top of their historical range. Cyclicals' valuations have fallen somewhat but are not priced for a slowdown.
The report cites 'some cracks in Q3 reporting' at banks, without figures.

tension_points.bull_case: Cyclicals' valuations have fallen and look more attractive relative to defensives. Past 12%-plus defensive outperformance, in March 2020 and July 2022, marked market troughs, so tactical cyclical opportunities may follow.
tension_points.bear_case: Cyclicals are not priced for the slowdown ahead. Credit spreads are widening, bank lending is tightening and the Fed is hiking, so the cycle is moving to a late stage.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A quick reversal in credit spreads would weaken the bear case. The bank sees that as less likely than in April 2025.
